<a id="concept-concurrency-parallelism"></a>

### Concurrency / Parallelism

**Area:** [Computer Systems and Software](#area-systems)

**Definition:** Concurrency allows tasks to make progress over overlapping periods; parallelism executes tasks simultaneously.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Asynchrony describes waiting and control flow and is not equivalent to parallelism.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Supports these next concepts:** [Backpressure / Subscriber Demand](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-backpressure) · [Adaptive Concurrency / Queue Estimation](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-adaptive-concurrency) · [MapReduce / Mergeable Summaries](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-mapreduce-combiners) · [Token Bucket / Rate Limiting](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-token-bucket) · [Message Ordering / FIFO Groups](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-message-ordering) · [GPU Coalescing / Scan / Reduction](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-gpu-parallel-algorithms)

<a id="concept-cpu-gpu"></a>

### CPU / GPU

**Area:** [Computer Systems and Software](#area-systems)

**Definition:** CPUs handle complex control flow and varied operations; GPUs excel at large workloads with many similar operations that can run in parallel.

**Explanation:**

Scenario and inputs: A program takes 100 seconds. A GPU can accelerate 80 seconds of work by 10×; the other 20 seconds remain unchanged. Initially ignore transfer overhead.

Step 1: The accelerated portion falls from 80 seconds to 8, giving 28 seconds in total.

Step 2: Overall speedup is 100/28≈3.57, not 10.

Step 3: Even eliminating all 80 seconds leaves 20 seconds, limiting speedup to 5×. Real transfers and scheduling also affect the result.

Result and explanation: Amdahl’s law shows why an individual kernel’s speedup must be assessed in the context of end-to-end runtime.

Pitfalls and limits: The analysis assumes fixed workload and accelerated fraction. Larger batches or another algorithm can change that fraction and require fresh measurement.

Try another condition: If only 10% of time can be accelerated, what is the limit even at infinite speed?

Self-check answer: 1/0.9≈1.11×.

**Boundary and distinctions:** GPUs are not faster for every task.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Supports these next concepts:** [GPU Coalescing / Scan / Reduction](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-gpu-parallel-algorithms)

<a id="concept-backpressure"></a>

### Backpressure / Subscriber Demand

**Area:** [Computer Systems and Software](#area-systems)

**Definition:** Backpressure lets a consumer signal how much work it can accept. In Combine, subscriber demand limits how many elements a subscription may deliver.

**Explanation:**

With finite demand, each delivered element consumes one credit. Explicit requests and the additional demand returned by receive add credits; returning none adds zero and does not cancel existing demand.

A PassthroughSubject does not buffer values for later demand. With one subscriber and zero demand, a sent value is dropped for that subscriber. Other publishers and buffering operators can have different policies.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Demand limits deliveries rather than elapsed-time request rate. Unlimited demand, cancellation, reentrant sends, multiple subscribers, and completion require their own protocol rules.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Concurrency / Parallelism](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-concurrency-parallelism) · [API — Application Programming Interface](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-api)

<a id="concept-max-min-fairness"></a>

### Max-min Fairness / Water Filling

**Area:** [Computer Systems and Software](#area-systems)

**Definition:** Max-min allocation protects smaller unsatisfied allocations before increasing larger ones. For one divisible resource with equal weights and demand caps, progressive water filling computes the allocation.

**Explanation:**

For capacity C >= 0 and demands d_i >= 0, allocate x_i = min(d_i, lambda), choosing a common water level so the total is min(C, sum d_i). A demand-capped consumer leaves the sharing set when its cap is reached.

Sort demands, satisfy the smallest cap when it is no greater than the remaining equal share, then divide the remaining capacity equally among active consumers. Sorting costs O(n log(n + 1)) time; the subsequent scan is linear.

**Boundary and distinctions:** This formula assumes equal weights and one divisible resource, without reservations, placement constraints, or indivisible jobs. Peloton's hierarchical, weighted, multi-resource scheduler has additional policies.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Operating System](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-operating-system) · [Greedy](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-greedy) · [Complexity](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-complexity)

**Official reference:** [Technical source](https://www.uber.com/us/en/blog/resource-scheduler-cluster-management-peloton/)

**Related English questions:**

<a id="concept-gpu-parallel-algorithms"></a>

### GPU Coalescing / Scan / Reduction

**Area:** [Computer Systems and Software](#area-systems)

**Definition:** GPU algorithms must coordinate memory access, participating threads, and dependency depth as well as total arithmetic work.

**Explanation:**

Coalescing groups neighboring lane accesses into memory transactions. Under the stated 32-byte segment model, 32 aligned four-byte contiguous loads touch four segments; a one-word shift touches five.

A work-efficient exclusive scan has O(n) work and O(log n) dependency depth. A reduction combines inputs into a total. Participation masks and synchronization are part of correctness; floating-point results can change with the reduction tree.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Operation count and dependency depth do not predict GPU wall time. Transaction rules depend on architecture, and warp masks do not supply values for absent lanes.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [CPU / GPU](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-cpu-gpu) · [Concurrency / Parallelism](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-concurrency-parallelism) · [Prefix Sum](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-prefix-sum)

<a id="concept-bfs-dfs"></a>

### BFS / DFS

**Area:** [Data Structures and Algorithms](#area-algorithms)

**Definition:** BFS explores vertices layer by layer; DFS explores one branch before backtracking.

**Explanation:**

Breadth-first search uses a queue to explore nodes one step away before those two steps away. When every edge has the same cost, it therefore finds a path with the fewest steps. Depth-first search uses recursion or an explicit stack to follow a path deeply and backtrack when needed. It suits dependency analysis, connectivity structure, and backtracking. Finding a path with DFS does not mean finding a shortest path. Both searches must track visited states to avoid looping indefinitely around cycles.

**Boundary and distinctions:** BFS finds paths with the fewest edges. These need not have minimum total cost when edge weights differ.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Graph Algorithms](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-graph-algorithms)

**Supports these next concepts:** [Multi-source BFS](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-multi-source-bfs) · [Graph Core / Degree Peeling](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-graph-core-peeling)

<a id="concept-dijkstra"></a>

### Dijkstra’s Algorithm

**Area:** [Data Structures and Algorithms](#area-algorithms)

**Definition:** Repeatedly settle the vertex with the smallest tentative distance and relax its outgoing edges.

**Explanation:**

Dijkstra's algorithm maintains the best distances discovered so far, repeatedly selects the nearest unfinalized node, and uses it to improve its neighbors' distances. With nonnegative edge weights, this nearest node can be finalized safely: extending a path cannot suddenly make it cheaper through a negative edge. Navigation and nonnegative-cost networks are typical uses. A priority queue accelerates selecting the next node. Dijkstra is not a universal shortest-path algorithm for arbitrary weighted graphs.

**Boundary and distinctions:** The standard algorithm is not generally valid when edges may have negative weights.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Bellman-Ford](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-bellman-ford) — Settling with nonnegative weights differs from repeated edge relaxation

<a id="concept-dynamic-programming"></a>

### Dynamic Programming

**Area:** [Data Structures and Algorithms](#area-algorithms)

**Definition:** Save reusable subproblem results and solve them according to defined states and transitions.

**Explanation:**

The central question in dynamic programming is not how to fill a table, but how to define the state. A state should retain information needed for future decisions without carrying irrelevant history. In a knapsack problem, for example, the current item and remaining capacity define the state; given these, the order in which earlier items were considered usually no longer matters.

If different choice sequences reach the same state, its best result can be computed once and reused: this is an overlapping subproblem. Optimization also requires that the current optimum can be constructed from suitable subproblem optima, usually called optimal substructure. Top-down memoization solves and caches states when encountered; bottom-up computation evaluates them in dependency order.

Examples include knapsack, longest common subsequence, edit distance, and certain path problems. The number of states can be enormous; adding several dimensions can cause state explosion. Dynamic programming does not make every combinatorial problem cheap. In an interview, explain that a suitable state definition merges subproblems that recur along different paths, using stored intermediate results to avoid repeated search.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Memoization alone is insufficient; state meanings and boundaries must also be clear.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-exact-decimal-arithmetic"></a>

### Exact Decimal Arithmetic / Minor Units

**Area:** [Data Structures and Algorithms](#area-algorithms)

**Definition:** A fixed-point representation stores an integer coefficient and an explicit decimal scale. Conversion must also respect the allowed increments of the target API operation.

**Explanation:**

Represent a value as m/10^s. To increase the scale, multiply m by a power of ten. To reduce it without rounding, require the discarded digits to be zero. Decimal-string operations can implement this conversion without a binary floating-point intermediate.

Keep the representation scale separate from the allowed amount quantum. Stripe represents ISK with two decimal places but permits only whole-ISK charges; HUF and TWD manual payouts similarly require minor-unit integers divisible by 100.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Representation scale and allowed increments can differ by operation. Input grammar, precision, and divisibility need separate checks. Integer storage must be wide enough; arbitrary-precision arithmetic does not have constant cost for unbounded digit counts.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Data Structures](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-data-structures) · [Loop Invariant](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-loop-invariant) · [API — Application Programming Interface](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-api)

<a id="concept-cryptographic-hash"></a>

### Cryptographic Hashes / Streaming Digests

**Area:** [Data Structures and Algorithms](#area-algorithms)

**Definition:** A cryptographic hash maps bytes to a fixed-size digest. Incremental hashing processes a byte stream in pieces while preserving the digest of their concatenation.

**Explanation:**

Dropbox content_hash first hashes each 4,194,304-byte block with SHA-256, then hashes the concatenation of the raw 32-byte block digests. Only the final digest is encoded as hexadecimal. Transport chunk boundaries do not change the fixed block boundaries.

Keep one inner hash context, one outer context, and a block-byte counter. Finalize every full block and any remaining nonempty block. An empty file contributes no inner block; an exact block multiple must not append an empty block.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Dropbox content_hash differs from SHA-256 applied directly to the file. Hash-table indexing, content identification, and authentication have different requirements. Digest equality is subject to collision assumptions and does not by itself authenticate a sender.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Data Structures](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-data-structures) · [Loop Invariant](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-loop-invariant) · [Complexity](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-complexity)

<a id="concept-unicode-graphemes"></a>

### Unicode Grapheme Clusters / UTF-8

**Area:** [Data Structures and Algorithms](#area-algorithms)

**Definition:** A user-perceived character, a Unicode scalar, and an encoded byte are different units. Swift Character represents an extended grapheme cluster; UTF-8 measures its encoded bytes.

**Explanation:**

The decomposed string e followed by a combining acute accent contains two Unicode scalars but one grapheme cluster and three UTF-8 bytes. A multi-scalar emoji can also form one Character.

For a byte-limited prefix that preserves characters, visit whole grapheme clusters in order and accumulate each cluster's UTF-8 length. Stop before the next cluster would exceed the budget. Segmentation should use a Unicode-aware library rather than byte slicing.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Counting characters does not give a byte length. Canonically equivalent text can have different byte sequences. The segmentation version and normalization policy are part of an interoperable text-processing contract.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Data Structures](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-data-structures) · [Loop Invariant](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-loop-invariant)

<a id="concept-floyd-warshall"></a>

### Floyd–Warshall / All-pairs Shortest Paths

**Area:** [Data Structures and Algorithms](#area-algorithms)

**Definition:** Floyd–Warshall computes shortest-path costs between every pair of vertices by expanding the set of permitted intermediate vertices.

**Explanation:**

Initialize d[i][i] = 0, direct edges to their minimum weight, and missing edges to infinity. For each intermediate vertex k, update d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]) for every i and j.

Keep k as the outer loop so each stage has a complete intermediate-vertex meaning. The algorithm uses O(V³) time and O(V²) storage for V vertices. A small alphabet of directed character conversions is a natural application.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Unreachable pairs remain infinite and must not be treated as free conversions. Negative cycles can make finite shortest-path costs undefined for affected pairs.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Graph Algorithms](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-graph-algorithms) · [Dynamic Programming](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-dynamic-programming)

**Official reference:** [Technical source](https://huggingface.co/datasets/hackercupai/hackercup/blob/209283d622e6ee41daa4a889d48f3cd67ebdab01/2021/quals/consistency_ch2.md)

<a id="concept-graph-core-peeling"></a>

### Graph Core / Degree Peeling

**Area:** [Data Structures and Algorithms](#area-algorithms)

**Definition:** For an undirected graph, the k-core is the greatest induced subgraph whose vertices all have degree at least k within that subgraph. Repeatedly removing vertices of degree below k finds it.

**Explanation:**

Initialize degrees and enqueue every vertex below the threshold. Removing a vertex reduces each surviving neighbor's degree; enqueue a neighbor when it becomes ineligible. Queue processing with adjacency lists takes O(V + E) time and O(V + E) total storage.

Any feasible induced subgraph with minimum degree at least k survives every removal: a vertex currently below k cannot belong to such a subgraph. This invariant proves both the pruning rule and the maximality of the remainder. A required vertex removed during peeling makes a constrained planting problem impossible.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Use current degrees after removals. Core membership differs from connected-component membership; even a 2-core can contain a bridge joining two cyclic regions.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [BFS / DFS](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-bfs-dfs) · [Graph Algorithms](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-graph-algorithms)

<a id="concept-squared-distance-moments"></a>

### Squared-distance Sums / Coordinate Moments

**Area:** [Data Structures and Algorithms](#area-algorithms)

**Definition:** Expanding squared Euclidean distance separates fixed point-set statistics from the query, turning a scan over all stored points into a constant-size calculation in fixed dimension.

**Explanation:**

For n points (x_i, y_i), retain Sx = Σx_i, Sy = Σy_i, and Q = Σ(x_i² + y_i²). At query (a, b), the total squared distance is n(a² + b²) − 2aSx − 2bSy + Q.

Build these moments in O(n) time and evaluate q two-dimensional queries in O(q) time, using O(1) aggregate state. With modular output, reduce the expanded expression consistently and use arithmetic wide enough for every product.

**Boundary and distinctions:** The expansion is for squared distances. It does not give the sum of ordinary Euclidean distances. Coordinates and aggregate products can exceed safe integer ranges even when each coordinate fits individually.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Prefix Sum](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-prefix-sum) · [Complexity](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-complexity)

<a id="concept-index"></a>

### Index

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** Maintain additional lookup structures to reduce the data that queries need to scan.

**Explanation:**

An inverted index maps a word or feature back to documents containing it, supporting keyword search. A bitmap index represents records with a particular value as bits, turning multiple-condition filtering into fast bitwise operations for certain analytical workloads. These are not more advanced B+ trees; they target different query structures. A database may maintain several indexes and let its planner choose among them. Ask about query conditions before choosing an index.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Query benefits come with write and storage maintenance costs.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-adaptive-concurrency"></a>

### Adaptive Concurrency / Queue Estimation

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** An adaptive concurrency limiter changes the allowed number of in-flight requests using observed service behavior. Latency relative to an unloaded baseline can estimate queue buildup.

**Explanation:**

For limit L, baseline latency R0, and sample latency R >= R0 > 0, Netflix's pinned Vegas implementation estimates queue size as ceil(L(1 - R0/R)). Its update also considers drops, utilization, configured thresholds, bounds, and smoothing.

The exercise fixes the baseline and policy to make each transition checkable. The full implementation also primes the baseline and periodically probes it; those branches can skip a normal limit update.

**Boundary and distinctions:** The queue estimate is a model, not a measured count of waiting requests. A concurrency cap is distinct from a request-rate quota. This pinned open-source implementation does not establish Netflix's current production configuration.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Concurrency / Parallelism](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-concurrency-parallelism) · [Network](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-network) · [Loop Invariant](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-loop-invariant)

<a id="concept-sql-aggregation"></a>

### SQL Aggregation / Join Cardinality

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** SQL aggregates summarize rows after filtering and joining. Correct counts depend on the unit being counted and the number of rows each join produces.

**Explanation:**

COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(expression) ignores NULL values, and COUNT(DISTINCT expression) counts distinct nonnull values. A left join creates a NULL-filled row for an unmatched parent; a one-to-many join can repeat each parent's values.

Group by stable identifiers when different entities can share a name. To return every maximum, compare each result with the maximum aggregate rather than selecting one arbitrary row. Compute percentages with the intended denominator and real-valued division; use ORDER BY when output order matters.

**Boundary and distinctions:** SQL does not promise row order without ORDER BY. Empty groups, NULL, duplicate join matches, and tied maxima need explicit contracts. Logical query semantics do not determine whether an engine uses hashing, sorting, or an index.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Data Structures](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-data-structures) · [Hash Table](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-hash-table) · [Index](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-index)

<a id="concept-mapreduce-combiners"></a>

### MapReduce / Mergeable Summaries

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** MapReduce groups intermediate values by key. Mergeable summaries reduce communication while retaining the information needed for a final result.

**Explanation:**

For a mean, retain (sum, count), combine pairs componentwise, and divide once at the end. An unweighted average of worker means fails when partition sizes differ.

A combiner must preserve results when applied to different groupings, including when it is skipped. Associativity and commutativity are useful requirements for unordered aggregation; floating-point rounding still depends on evaluation order.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Aggregation algebra does not by itself guarantee exactly-once side effects, deterministic floating-point results, or balanced partitions.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Replication / Sharding](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-replication-sharding) · [Concurrency / Parallelism](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-concurrency-parallelism)

<a id="concept-mergeable-variance"></a>

### Mergeable Variance / Welford Summaries

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** A variance summary retains count n, mean mu, and centered squared-deviation sum M2. These statistics can be merged without retaining every observation.

**Explanation:**

For nonempty summaries A and B, let n = nA + nB and delta = muB - muA. Merge with mu = muA + delta*nB/n and M2 = M2A + M2B + delta^2*nA*nB/n. An empty summary is the identity and needs a separate branch before division.

Population variance is M2/n for n > 0. Averaging shard variances misses variation between shard means. Each summary merge uses constant arithmetic work and state; a stream can update the same statistics one observation at a time.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Population variance and sample variance use different denominators. Empty input needs an explicit convention. Floating-point overflow and rounding remain possible, and different merge orders can produce slightly different results.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [MapReduce / Mergeable Summaries](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-mapreduce-combiners) · [Complexity](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-complexity)

**Official reference:** [Technical source](https://github.com/airbnb/chronon/blob/5bbc4d176a205e32b4172b8f0ecd360072cdb0fe/aggregator/src/main/scala/ai/chronon/aggregator/base/SimpleAggregators.scala#L160-L247)

<a id="concept-external-consistency"></a>

### External Consistency

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** External consistency orders transactions serially while preserving real-time precedence: a transaction completed before another begins must precede it in the serial order.

**Explanation:**

Serializability requires equivalence to a serial transaction order. External consistency adds the order that clients can observe between non-overlapping transactions.

If T1 commits before T2 begins, a consistent snapshot cannot include T2's effects while omitting T1's. Strong reads started after both commits must reflect both; an explicitly historical snapshot can precede them.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Two independent reads are not automatically one snapshot. Clock timestamps alone do not establish a transaction consistency guarantee.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Transaction / ACID](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-transaction-acid) · [Consensus](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-consensus)

**Official reference:** [Technical source](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/true-time-external-consistency)

<a id="concept-slo-error-budget"></a>

### SLI / SLO / Error Budget

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** An SLI measures a service property. An SLO sets its target. An error budget quantifies the failures allowed under a specified target and measurement window.

**Explanation:**

For N > 0 eligible requests, B bad requests, and success target S, observed success is 1 − B/N and the allowed bad-event count is N(1 − S). Budget consumption is B/[N(1 − S)] when the denominator is positive.

Define eligible events, observation window, and measurement location before calculating the ratio. A request-based budget and a time-based availability budget have different denominators.

**Boundary and distinctions:** A request error fraction cannot be converted directly into outage duration. An SLO target alone is not an SLA with contractual consequences.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Network](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-network)

**Official reference:** [Technical source](https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/)

<a id="concept-token-bucket"></a>

### Token Bucket / Rate Limiting

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** A token bucket limits sustained admission while allowing bounded bursts. Requests consume credit that refills at a fixed rate up to a capacity.

**Explanation:**

For capacity C, rate r, elapsed time Δt, and previous credit b, refill to min(C, b + rΔt). Admit a unit-cost request only when this balance is at least one, then subtract one.

Retain fractional credit and update the timestamp on each refill. Shared buckets need atomic refill-and-consume decisions; independent replica buckets do not enforce one global quota.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Rate, concurrent in-flight work, and queue size are different limits. A token bucket is not a guarantee of uniform spacing between requests.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Network](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-network) · [Concurrency / Parallelism](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-concurrency-parallelism)

**Official reference:** [Technical source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/throttling)

<a id="concept-circuit-breaker"></a>

### Circuit Breaker

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** A circuit breaker temporarily rejects calls to an unhealthy dependency, then permits bounded probes to test recovery.

**Explanation:**

Closed allows calls and records outcomes. Open rejects locally until the recovery policy permits a transition. Half-open allows limited trial calls before restoring normal traffic or reopening.

Choose explicit failure thresholds, observation windows, timeout behavior, and recovery criteria. Concurrent callers must coordinate probe admission to avoid releasing a new burst into a failing service.

**Boundary and distinctions:** A circuit breaker does not make retries safe, replace a timeout, or enforce a request-rate quota. Local rejections are not downstream failures.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Network](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-network)

**Official reference:** [Technical source](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker)

<a id="concept-optimistic-concurrency"></a>

### Optimistic Concurrency / Conditional Writes

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** Optimistic concurrency detects conflicts when a write commits. A conditional write changes state only if a version or state predicate still holds atomically.

**Explanation:**

A version check such as If-Match rejects a stale replacement. After a conflict, reread the current state and recompute the intended change before retrying.

A state predicate can enforce a local invariant directly, such as stock >= requested quantity before subtracting stock in the same atomic operation.

**Boundary and distinctions:** A separate read and write do not provide an atomic condition. Conditional mutation alone does not deduplicate repeated business requests or establish a multi-item transaction.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Transaction / ACID](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-transaction-acid)

**Supports these next concepts:** [Idempotency / Safe Retries](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-idempotency) · [Distributed Cache Coherence / Leases](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-cache-coherence)

<a id="concept-idempotency"></a>

### Idempotency / Safe Retries

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** An idempotent operation has the same intended effect when repeated as when applied once. A request identifier can extend this property to operations with business side effects.

**Explanation:**

A lost response leaves the caller uncertain whether an operation committed. Retrying a decrement can apply the change twice even if every individual decrement is atomic.

Bind an idempotency key to the request intent. Coordinate recording that key, applying the mutation, and retaining its result so duplicate submissions return the earlier outcome. Define key scope, retention, and behavior for the same key with different parameters.

**Boundary and distinctions:** A timeout does not prove failure. A stock predicate, transport retry, FIFO delivery, or expiring cache entry alone does not guarantee one business effect.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Transaction / ACID](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-transaction-acid) · [Optimistic Concurrency / Conditional Writes](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-optimistic-concurrency)

**Official reference:** [Technical source](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/)

<a id="concept-message-ordering"></a>

### Message Ordering / FIFO Groups

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** A message group defines an ordering boundary. Independent groups can make progress concurrently without a total order across all messages.

**Explanation:**

If A1 precedes A2 and B1 precedes B2, six complete interleavings respect these two constraints: choose the two A positions from four slots.

Choose grouping keys that match the business invariant, then process effects in group order. Delivery, handler completion, visibility timeouts, and duplicate effects require separate reasoning.

**Boundary and distinctions:** FIFO delivery does not serialize arbitrary asynchronous side effects. A mathematical set of valid schedules does not promise that a queue implements every schedule.

<a id="concept-consistent-hashing"></a>

### Consistent Hashing

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** Consistent hashing maps keys and routing tokens into one stable hash space so membership changes move a limited ownership range.

**Explanation:**

In a clockwise ring, a key belongs to the first token at or after its hash, with wraparound. A sorted token array supports this lookup with binary search.

Inserting a token transfers the interval from the previous token, exclusive, to the new token, inclusive. Virtual tokens can improve balance; replication must select distinct physical owners when required.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Limited remapping does not imply equal load, automatic data migration, or consistency during reconfiguration. One hot key can remain a bottleneck.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Replication / Sharding](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-replication-sharding) · [Lower Bound / Upper Bound](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-lower-bound-upper-bound)

<a id="concept-cache-coherence"></a>

### Distributed Cache Coherence / Leases

**Area:** [Databases, Networks, and Distributed Systems](#area-infrastructure)

**Definition:** Distributed cache coherence concerns how cached values track authoritative updates. A fill lease can reject an old in-flight read after invalidation.

**Explanation:**

In cache-aside, a reader can miss, read an old database value, pause, and refill after a writer commits and deletes the cache entry. Deleting after the database write does not eliminate that interleaving.

Grant a per-key fill token and invalidate it on deletion. Check the token atomically when accepting a fill. A delayed reader with an invalid token cannot repopulate that entry with its old value.

**Boundary and distinctions:** This lease protects the illustrated stale-fill race. It is not a CPU cache-coherence protocol, a normal TTL, or a proof of globally serializable database and cache reads.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Cache](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-cache) · [Optimistic Concurrency / Conditional Writes](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-optimistic-concurrency)

**Official reference:** [Technical source](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi13/nsdi13-final170_update.pdf)

<a id="concept-binary-multiclass-multilabel"></a>

### Binary / Multiclass / Multilabel

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** Distinguish two possible outcomes, one choice among mutually exclusive classes, and multiple labels that may hold simultaneously.

**Explanation:**

Binary classification answers a yes/no question, such as whether an email is spam. Multiclass single-label classification chooses one of several mutually exclusive answers, such as cat, dog, or bird as the main species. Multilabel classification allows several answers simultaneously, such as both cats and dogs in an image. It usually assigns each label a separate probability without requiring them to sum to one. This distinction directly affects the output layer and loss; class count alone cannot determine whether BCE or mutually exclusive categorical cross-entropy is appropriate.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Determine the task semantics before selecting outputs and loss.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Sample / Feature / Label](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-sample-feature-label)

<a id="concept-broadcasting"></a>

### Broadcasting

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** Use shape rules to extend the meaning of operations on smaller tensors without explicit copying.

**Explanation:**

Dtype is the numeric representation, such as integer or floating point. Device specifies where data and computation reside, such as CPU or GPU. Broadcasting lets smaller-shaped data participate in operations with larger-shaped data under defined rules, without manually copying it—for example, adding the same bias to each feature across a batch. Broadcasting can also make an incorrectly shaped computation run, so absence of an error does not prove correctness. Padding fills positions in unequal-length sequences; a mask tells computation which positions are valid.

**Boundary and distinctions:** A valid broadcast can still compute the wrong quantity.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Tensor / Shape / Axis](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-tensor-shape-axis)

<a id="concept-calibration"></a>

### Calibration

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** Check whether the reported probabilities match the actual long-term occurrence rates.

**Explanation:**

Calibration asks whether reported probabilities are trustworthy: among events assigned an 80% probability, do about 80% occur over the long run? A model can rank well yet produce overconfident probabilities, giving high AUC but poor calibration. The Brier score measures the difference between probabilities and binary outcomes. Temperature scaling adjusts output score magnitudes while preserving some ranking structure, and is often used for post-hoc calibration. Fit it on appropriately held-out data. Do not use test labels to improve the model and then report the same test as an independent evaluation.

**Boundary and distinctions:** A high AUC does not guarantee well-calibrated probabilities.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Cross-Validation](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-cross-validation) — Calibration also needs appropriate held-out data
- [ROC AUC / PR AUC](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-roc-auc-pr-auc) — Ranking quality differs from probability calibration

<a id="concept-cross-validation"></a>

### Cross-Validation

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** Evaluate a training procedure across several data splits, using nested validation when model selection must be isolated.

**Explanation:**

Cross-validation evaluates stability across repeated data splits. Out-of-fold predictions, or OOF predictions, come from a fold model that did not see the corresponding sample during training; stacking commonly uses them. Nested cross-validation performs model selection in an inner loop and evaluates the whole selection procedure in an outer loop, reducing optimism from repeated tuning. It costs more computation and does not eliminate distribution shift. The time-based or group-based splitting rules must still be appropriate.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Time-dependent or grouped data cannot be split randomly without considering its structure.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Data Leakage](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-data-leakage) — Fit preprocessing statistics within each training split
- [Calibration](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-calibration) — Calibration also needs appropriate held-out data

<a id="concept-f1"></a>

### F1 Score

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** Combine precision and recall through their harmonic mean; a low value of either limits F1.

**Explanation:**

Suppose 100 of 1,000 emails are spam. The model flags 80 emails, of which 60 are actually spam. There are therefore 60 true positives, 20 false positives, 40 false negatives and 880 true negatives. Precision is 60/80=75%; recall is 60/100=60%; F1 is about 66.7%; accuracy is 94%.

On the same data, predicting every email as legitimate gives 90% accuracy but finds no spam. This shows why metrics must match the task. Select a threshold on validation data using the costs of false alarms and missed detections. Do not choose the best threshold on the test set and then call its score an independent test result.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Specify averaging conventions such as macro or micro when comparing multiclass results.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Precision](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-precision) — Precision is an input to F1
- [Recall](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-recall) — Recall is an input to F1
- [Macro / Micro](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-macro-micro) — Specify the averaging convention for F1

**Related English questions:**

<a id="concept-logit"></a>

### Logit

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** In neural classification, a logit is usually a raw score before sigmoid or softmax.

**Explanation:**

In neural-network classification, a logit usually means a raw score before conversion to probability; it may be negative or exceed one. Sigmoid maps one score to a value between zero and one, often for whether a label holds. Softmax converts a set of scores to probabilities summing to one, distributing probability across mutually exclusive classes. These are output transformations, not complete learning algorithms or loss functions. A high probability does not ensure correctness, because calibration may be poor.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Scores may be negative or exceed one; they are not probabilities.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Binary / Multiclass / Multilabel](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-binary-multiclass-multilabel)

**Supports these next concepts:** [BCEWithLogitsLoss](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-bcewithlogitsloss)

**Related connections:**

- [Sigmoid](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-sigmoid) — A scalar score can become a binary probability
- [Softmax](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-softmax) — Softmax converts scores into probabilities over mutually exclusive classes

<a id="concept-macro-micro"></a>

### Macro / Micro

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** Macro averaging computes each class metric and takes their equally weighted mean; micro averaging pools counts before computing the metric.

**Explanation:**

For multiclass or multilabel tasks, metrics can be calculated separately for each class and then averaged. Macro averaging gives every class equal weight, making problems in small classes easier to see. Weighted averaging uses weights such as class sample counts, so large classes can dominate. Micro averaging pools the counts first, then calculates the metric, emphasizing overall sample-level performance. All three scores may be called F1 but differ, so comparisons must specify the averaging method.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Class-frequency-weighted averaging is a separate convention affected by class sample counts.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [F1 Score](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-f1) — Specify the averaging convention for F1

<a id="concept-parameter-hyperparameter"></a>

### Parameter / Hyperparameter

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** Parameters are obtained by fitting, and hyperparameters usually control the model structure or training method.

**Explanation:**

Weights and biases are learnable model values; “parameter” is the general category. Learning rate, batch size, and maximum tree depth are usually hyperparameters controlling the model or training, rather than weights directly fitted by ordinary training. A bias term is not the statistical bias in the bias–variance tradeoff or social bias. The same word has different meanings: first determine whether the discussion concerns model structure, statistical error, or fairness.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Learning rate and batch size are usually hyperparameters.

<a id="concept-precision"></a>

### Precision

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** Among examples predicted positive, the fraction that are actually positive: TP/(TP+FP).

**Explanation:**

Suppose 100 of 1,000 emails are spam. The model flags 80 emails, of which 60 are actually spam. There are therefore 60 true positives, 20 false positives, 40 false negatives and 880 true negatives. Precision is 60/80=75%; recall is 60/100=60%; F1 is about 66.7%; accuracy is 94%.

On the same data, predicting every email as legitimate gives 90% accuracy but finds no spam. This shows why metrics must match the task. Select a threshold on validation data using the costs of false alarms and missed detections. Do not choose the best threshold on the test set and then call its score an independent test result.

**Boundary and distinctions:** The denominator counts predicted positives, not actual positives. Precision is undefined when no examples are predicted positive unless a reporting convention is specified.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Threshold](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-threshold) — Thresholds change the composition of predicted positives
- [F1 Score](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-f1) — Precision is an input to F1

<a id="concept-recall"></a>

### Recall

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** Among actual positive examples, the fraction predicted positive: TP/(TP+FN). Also called sensitivity or true positive rate.

**Explanation:**

Suppose 100 of 1,000 emails are spam. The model flags 80 emails, of which 60 are actually spam. There are therefore 60 true positives, 20 false positives, 40 false negatives and 880 true negatives. Precision is 60/80=75%; recall is 60/100=60%; F1 is about 66.7%; accuracy is 94%.

On the same data, predicting every email as legitimate gives 90% accuracy but finds no spam. This shows why metrics must match the task. Select a threshold on validation data using the costs of false alarms and missed detections. Do not choose the best threshold on the test set and then call its score an independent test result.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Improving recall does not mean false positives are necessarily acceptable.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-sample-feature-label"></a>

### Sample / Feature / Label

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** A sample is a learning instance, features are available inputs, and a label is a supervised target.

**Explanation:**

A sample is one example, such as an order. A feature is information available for prediction, such as price or a user's previous view count. A label is a supervised answer, such as whether the order was later canceled. Target is a broader term for the value or content the model is trained to predict or reconstruct: a class, number, next text segment, or image. Labels need not be manually annotated: next-word prediction gets its answers from the text itself. Distinguish answers available during training from information available at prediction time. If an answer unavailable at prediction time enters the input during training or evaluation, it causes data leakage.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Information unavailable at prediction time causes leakage if included among features.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Supports these next concepts:** [Feature Engineering](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-feature-engineering) · [Binary / Multiclass / Multilabel](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-binary-multiclass-multilabel)

<a id="concept-tensor-shape-axis"></a>

### Tensor / Shape / Axis

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** A tensor organizes multidimensional data, its shape lists axis sizes, and an axis identifies a direction of organization or computation.

**Explanation:**

For now, think of a tensor as a multidimensional array. Its shape gives its size along each direction; an axis identifies a direction of organization or computation. A color-image batch can have sample, channel, height, and width axes. “Dimension” may mean the number of axes or the size of one axis, so context matters. Embedding dimension usually means components per vector, not dataset sample count. Shape mismatches concern data alignment, not necessarily a flaw in the algorithm's principle.

**Boundary and distinctions:** “Dimension” may mean the number of axes or the size of one axis; check context.

<a id="concept-threshold"></a>

### Threshold

**Area:** [Data, Tasks, and Evaluation](#area-data-evaluation)

**Definition:** Turn a probability or score into a hard classification decision using a cutoff.

**Explanation:**

A classification threshold must still be chosen after predicting probabilities. Raising it usually produces fewer positive predictions but may miss more actual positives. The confusion matrix distinguishes true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives. Sensitivity usually means recall, or the true positive rate. Specificity measures the proportion of actual negatives correctly excluded. These measure different aspects of performance and should be discussed in terms of missed detections and false alarms.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Choose thresholds on validation data according to false-positive and false-negative costs.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Precision](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-precision) — Thresholds change the composition of predicted positives
- [Recall](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-recall) — Thresholds change how many true positives are found

<a id="concept-boosting"></a>

### Boosting

**Area:** [Machine Learning and Statistical Models](#area-ml-methods)

**Definition:** Add models in successive rounds to improve their combination; methods differ in objectives and weighting rules.

**Explanation:**

Gradient boosting adds models sequentially to improve the current ensemble. With squared error, a new tree can be understood as predicting unexplained residuals; with other losses, fitting negative loss gradients is more accurate. GBDT uses decision trees as gradient-boosting base learners. Each round adds a correction rather than training a wholly independent complete model.

The learning rate controls each new tree's contribution; tree count controls the number of rounds. Smaller contributions often require more rounds to reach a given training error, so consider both together. Maximum depth and leaf count constrain each correction's complexity. Training corrections do not guarantee improvement on validation every round, so early stopping is common.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Boosting methods cannot all be described as fitting the same type of residual.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Random Forest](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-random-forest) — Parallel diversity differs from sequential improvement

<a id="concept-bootstrap-oob"></a>

### Bootstrap / OOB

**Area:** [Machine Learning and Statistical Models](#area-ml-methods)

**Definition:** Sample with replacement to form training data. A tree can evaluate examples not selected in its bootstrap sample.

**Explanation:**

Bootstrap sampling draws training examples with replacement, so some repeat and others are omitted. Bagging trains models on different resamples and combines their predictions, hoping their incidental errors partly cancel. Copying the same model repeatedly does not help: if all models make identical errors, averaging cannot fix them. Diversity and individual model quality both matter.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Out-of-bag evaluation does not replace appropriate temporal or group-based validation.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

<a id="concept-em-viterbi"></a>

### EM / Viterbi

**Area:** [Machine Learning and Statistical Models](#area-ml-methods)

**Definition:** EM iteratively estimates parameters in models with latent variables; Viterbi finds the most likely hidden-state sequence for a given model.

**Explanation:**

Latent variables are unobserved internal variables used to explain data—for example, a customer's unknown group given observed spending. EM alternates estimating hidden-variable probabilities under current parameters and updating parameters using those estimates. In a GMM, it repeatedly estimates component memberships and updates the components. Under suitable conditions the objective does not worsen, but a global optimum is not guaranteed.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Estimating model parameters differs from decoding a hidden-state sequence.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

<a id="concept-knn-k-means"></a>

### KNN / K-means

**Area:** [Machine Learning and Statistical Models](#area-ml-methods)

**Definition:** KNN predicts using labeled neighbors; K-means finds a specified number of centers in unlabeled data.

**Explanation:**

K-means fixes the number of clusters, alternates assignment to the nearest center with updates from cluster members, and suits compact groups under the chosen features and distance. It cannot fit arbitrary cluster shapes. K-means++ improves initialization by spreading centers apart, but does not guarantee a global optimum. Feature scales affect distance, so do not combine customer income and age without considering their units.

**Boundary and distinctions:** KNN is covered in Chapter 29. Similar names do not imply the same task.

<a id="concept-pca"></a>

### PCA — Principal Component Analysis

**Area:** [Machine Learning and Statistical Models](#area-ml-methods)

**Definition:** Find orthogonal directions of maximum variance, usually after centering the data, to construct a lower-dimensional linear representation.

**Explanation:**

PCA finds linear directions of greatest variation, retaining as much overall variation as possible with fewer coordinates. It supports compression, denoising, and preprocessing, but greatest variance is not necessarily most predictive: class differences may lie in low-variance directions. Standard PCA uses no supervised labels and does not guarantee preservation of classification-relevant information. Input scales influence results; whether to standardize depends on the task.

**Boundary and distinctions:** High-variance directions need not be the most useful for classification.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Multimodal Representation](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-multimodal-representation) — Representation tasks differ in supervision and objectives

<a id="concept-random-forest"></a>

### Random Forest

**Area:** [Machine Learning and Statistical Models](#area-ml-methods)

**Definition:** Train trees using random sample selection and candidate features, then aggregate their predictions.

**Explanation:**

Random forests predict with many trees. Classic training gives each tree a different bootstrap sample and limits each split to a random feature subset. This second randomness is crucial: if one strong feature always dominates the top split, trees become similar; limiting candidates lets them explore different rules.

Regression usually averages tree values; classification may vote or average class probabilities depending on implementation. Different perspectives reduce a single tree's high variance. They cannot recover information every tree lacks, nor guarantee freedom from overfitting.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Random forests mainly reduce variance; they do not guarantee freedom from overfitting.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Decision Tree](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-decision-tree)

<a id="concept-activation-checkpointing"></a>

### Activation Checkpointing

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Store fewer intermediate activations and recompute them during backpropagation, trading computation time for GPU memory.

**Explanation:**

Activation checkpointing avoids saving every intermediate activation and recomputes some during backpropagation, trading extra computation for GPU memory. A model checkpoint instead saves model or training state for recovery or deployment. Both use the word checkpoint, but solve different problems. Gradient accumulation, parameter sharding and freezing some parameters can also reduce GPU memory use, each with computational or capability tradeoffs.

**Boundary and distinctions:** This differs from saving a model checkpoint for recovery.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

<a id="concept-adagrad-rmsprop"></a>

### Adagrad / RMSProp

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Adagrad accumulates squared gradients; RMSProp uses an exponential moving average of squared gradients to adapt per-parameter update scales.

**Explanation:**

AdaGrad scales each parameter’s update using its past gradients. This is useful for sparse features, but cumulative statistics can make effective step sizes increasingly small. RMSProp uses moving averages of recent squared gradients to limit that continual decay. These are adaptive step-size methods: parameters can receive different effective update scales. Adaptive does not mean that the learning rate needs no tuning or that validation is unnecessary.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Adaptation still requires setting and validating the learning rate.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-adam-adamw"></a>

### Adam / AdamW

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Adam uses first- and second-moment estimates of gradients to scale updates; AdamW applies weight decay separately from that adaptive scaling.

**Explanation:**

Adam combines a moving average of gradients with statistics of squared gradients, giving both momentum and per-parameter scaling. Its beta parameters control how long past information is retained. Epsilon is a small numerical stabilizer, not an exploration probability. Check the context when the same parameter name appears in different algorithms. Adam is convenient for many deep learning tasks but is not universally the best optimizer in theory or practice.

**Boundary and distinctions:** AdamW changes how weight decay is applied; it is not simply a faster version of Adam.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [SGD / Momentum](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-sgd-momentum) — Historical directions differ from per-parameter scaling

<a id="concept-batch-size"></a>

### Batch Size

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** The number of samples processed in one forward pass. Gradient accumulation and data parallelism can increase the effective batch size used for an update.

**Explanation:**

A batch is a collection of samples processed together, and batch size is its sample count. An iteration usually means one execution of the training loop, although the code’s definition matters. An optimizer step is an actual parameter update. An epoch usually means one complete pass through a finite training dataset.

With 1,000 training samples and batches of 100, dropping no samples and updating once per batch gives ten batches and ten parameter updates per epoch. This is one epoch with ten update steps, not ten epochs. With streaming corpora or very large datasets, researchers may report optimizer steps or tokens processed rather than complete passes through the data.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Distinguish between per-device micro-batches and global effective batches.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Supports these next concepts:** [Microbatch / Gradient Accumulation](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-microbatch-gradient-accumulation)

<a id="concept-batchnorm-layernorm-rmsnorm"></a>

### BatchNorm / LayerNorm / RMSNorm

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Normalize activations using different statistical scopes and formulas to change network computation and training behavior.

**Explanation:**

Batch normalization uses minibatch statistics to normalize intermediate activations, then applies learnable parameters to preserve expressive capacity. It is common in convolutional networks. Very small training batches or large differences between devices’ batches can make the statistics unstable. Inference usually uses running statistics accumulated during training, rather than statistics from the current individual sample. Incorrect training or evaluation modes can therefore change outputs unexpectedly.

**Boundary and distinctions:** During training, BatchNorm typically uses minibatch statistics. LayerNorm normalizes features within each sample; RMSNorm does not subtract the mean.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-bce"></a>

### BCE — Binary Cross-Entropy

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Score binary probability predictions, penalizing confident rejection of the true outcome more strongly.

**Explanation:**

BCE is commonly used for binary classification and for each label in multilabel learning. It compares predicted probabilities with target labels, rather than merely counting correct class decisions. Think of it as scoring probability predictions: the less probability assigned to the true answer, the greater the penalty.

Consider an email that is actually spam. Model A assigns a 49% probability of spam; model B assigns only 1%. With a 50% classification threshold, both are wrong, so accuracy cannot distinguish these errors. But model B almost rules out the true answer and is more confidently wrong, so BCE penalizes it more. Probability prediction quality and the final hard classification are different things.

In multilabel image recognition, the model can separately predict whether an image contains a cat, a dog or a car, then combine the BCE losses for those labels. Separate loss terms do not imply that the labels are independent in the real world; a shared network can still use their correlations. If exactly one of cat, dog or bird must be chosen, model the classes as mutually exclusive instead.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Used for binary classification and per-label multilabel tasks; it measures more than thresholded correctness.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Sigmoid](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-sigmoid) — BCE without a fused sigmoid takes predicted probabilities
- [BCEWithLogitsLoss](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-bcewithlogitsloss) — A numerically stable fusion of the same objective
- [Cross-Entropy / NLL](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-cross-entropy-nll) — BCE is binary cross-entropy, related to classification NLL

<a id="concept-bcewithlogitsloss"></a>

### BCEWithLogitsLoss

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Accept logits directly and combine sigmoid with BCE in a numerically stable computation.

**Explanation:**

BCELoss expects probabilities as input. BCEWithLogitsLoss accepts raw logits and combines sigmoid with BCE internally. This fused computation improves numerical stability by avoiding problems caused by first forming extreme probabilities. Do not apply sigmoid separately before BCEWithLogitsLoss. You need not memorize the API for an interview, but should understand that WithLogits means scores before the probability transformation.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Targets should be floating-point tensors with matching shape. Do not apply sigmoid to the input again.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Logit](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-logit)

<a id="concept-checkpoint-resume-seed"></a>

### Checkpoint / Resume / Seed

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Save training state to resume later; seeds help control random processes.

**Explanation:**

A checkpoint saves training state. Model weights alone are usually sufficient for inference. Resuming training faithfully may also require optimizer state, scheduler progress, random-number-generator state and the data-loading position. A random seed helps control initialization and data shuffling, but hardware differences and nondeterministic operations can still change results. Reproducibility concerns the whole process, not just recording a seed.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Weights alone usually do not support exact continuation, and seeds do not guarantee identical results across environments.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-contrastive-loss"></a>

### Contrastive Loss

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Learn useful representations from positive and negative relationships or other contrastive structures.

**Explanation:**

Metric learning studies similarity in a representation space. Contrastive loss brings related representations closer while separating unrelated ones. Triplet loss uses an anchor, a positive sample and a negative sample, aiming to place the positive closer to the anchor than the negative. InfoNCE often frames learning as finding the correct match among a batch of candidates. These ideas support image–text alignment, semantic retrieval and face verification. Negative samples may actually be related to the anchor; such false negatives create misleading training pressure.

**Boundary and distinctions:** The definition of positive and negative pairs is itself a key assumption.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Multimodal Representation](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-multimodal-representation) — Contrastive objectives can align modalities

<a id="concept-cross-entropy-nll"></a>

### Cross-Entropy / NLL

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Classification cross-entropy relates to the negative log probability of the true class; NLL applies to more general likelihood models.

**Explanation:**

Cross-entropy is not an alternative to BCE: BCE is cross-entropy for the binary case. In training code, CrossEntropyLoss commonly accepts raw scores for multiple classes and performs the appropriate normalization internally. A typical task has one correct class per sample. Next-token prediction uses the same kind of classification objective over the vocabulary. Negative log-likelihood, or NLL, penalizes a model for assigning low likelihood to observed data. Cross-entropy for discrete classification is closely related to NLL, but likelihood-based objectives are not limited to classification.

**Boundary and distinctions:** PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss expects raw scores, while NLLLoss expects log probabilities.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [BCE — Binary Cross-Entropy](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-bce) — BCE is binary cross-entropy, related to classification NLL

<a id="concept-ctc"></a>

### CTC — Connectionist Temporal Classification

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Sum the probabilities of valid alignment paths when sequence labels are not aligned to individual input time steps.

**Explanation:**

CTC, connectionist temporal classification, handles tasks where input frames and output labels lack a known alignment. In speech recognition, for example, the transcript may be known without knowing which frames correspond to each sound. CTC sums over possible alignments using a collapse rule that merges consecutive repeated labels before removing a dedicated blank symbol. Label smoothing softens the target distribution to discourage overconfidence. Auxiliary losses add training signals for intermediate representations, load balancing or other goals. Adding a loss does not automatically help; objectives and their weights can conflict.

**Boundary and distinctions:** CTC assumes monotonic alignments and compatible sequence lengths; it does not align arbitrary sequence pairs.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-dice-loss"></a>

### Dice Loss

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Define a training objective from the overlap between predicted and target regions, commonly for segmentation.

**Explanation:**

IoU, intersection over union, measures overlap between predicted and ground-truth regions. Dice is another common overlap measure and can be used to construct a training loss. In medical imaging, a model may miss a small lesion entirely yet achieve high pixel accuracy by correctly predicting the background. Region-overlap metrics make this failure easier to see. Segmentation often combines BCE or cross-entropy with Dice-based objectives to assess both individual pixels and overall overlap. Distinguish differentiable training approximations from the metrics used in formal evaluation.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Smoothing terms and reduction conventions differ across implementations and affect the result.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-dropout"></a>

### Dropout

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Randomly mask some activations during training to reduce dependence on particular pathways.

**Explanation:**

Dropout randomly masks activations during training to reduce reliance on particular information pathways. Inference normally disables this masking, with scaling handled according to the implementation. Dropout does not permanently delete neurons after training. Drop path and stochastic depth randomly skip paths or residual branches in suitable architectures, providing more structured stochastic regularization. Their benefit depends on the architecture and data; adding more does not always help.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Standard inference does not permanently delete neurons.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-early-stopping-patience"></a>

### Early Stopping / Patience

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Stop according to validation performance; patience specifies how long improvement may be absent.

**Explanation:**

During training, periodically evaluate on validation data that was not used to fit the model. Falling training error alongside persistently worsening validation error is a common sign of overfitting. Early stopping ends training based on validation performance and usually retains a better checkpoint. Patience is the allowed number of consecutive checks without improvement, not necessarily seconds or epochs. Repeatedly using the test set to decide when to stop destroys its value as an independent evaluation.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Patience usually counts validation checks, so state its unit.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Regularization](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-regularization) — Validation performance can control training duration

<a id="concept-focal-loss"></a>

### Focal Loss

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Reduce the relative contribution of easy samples so that training focuses more on difficult samples.

**Explanation:**

Focal loss reduces the relative loss contribution of easy, correctly classified samples so that training focuses more on difficult ones. This is useful in object detection, where easy background locations can greatly outnumber objects. Rather than assigning a fixed minority-class weight, it adjusts a sample’s contribution according to the model’s current prediction. Difficult samples may also be mislabeled, so focal loss is not a universal remedy for class imbalance. Assess it alongside label quality, sampling and evaluation metrics.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Difficult examples may be mislabeled. Emphasizing them does not guarantee better performance.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-forward-backward"></a>

### Forward / Backward

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Compute predictions forward through a graph and loss gradients with respect to parameters backward through it.

**Explanation:**

The forward pass maps inputs to predictions. The loss function compares predictions with targets. Backpropagation computes how each parameter affects the loss: its gradient. The optimizer then updates parameters using those gradients and its own state. Backpropagation calculates gradients rather than updating parameters. Adam and SGD are update methods, rather than alternative network architectures. This sequence is fundamental to understanding training code.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Backpropagation does not itself update parameters.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Loss / Objective / Metric](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-loss-objective-metric)

**Related connections:**

- [Gradient](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-gradient) — Backpropagation computes parameter gradients

<a id="concept-gradient"></a>

### Gradient

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Describe the local rate of change along each parameter direction, guiding how updates affect loss.

**Explanation:**

The forward pass maps inputs to predictions. The loss function compares predictions with targets. Backpropagation computes how each parameter affects the loss: its gradient. The optimizer then updates parameters using those gradients and its own state. Backpropagation calculates gradients rather than updating parameters. Adam and SGD are update methods, rather than alternative network architectures. This sequence is fundamental to understanding training code.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Gradient direction and the eventual update size are different quantities.

<a id="concept-gradient-clipping"></a>

### Gradient Clipping

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Limit a gradient norm or its components to reduce instability from unusually large gradients.

**Explanation:**

Gradient clipping limits the magnitude of gradients in an update. Norm-based clipping commonly rescales the whole gradient when its norm is too large, preserving its overall direction; value-based clipping bounds individual components. This differs from reducing the learning rate: clipping targets unusually large gradients, whereas the learning rate sets the overall scale of updates. Excessive clipping can slow learning. It cannot compensate for incorrect labels or a faulty loss implementation.

**Boundary and distinctions:** With gradient scaling, normally unscale before clipping.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Mixed Precision / Loss Scaling](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-mixed-precision-loss-scaling) — Unscale gradients before clipping

<a id="concept-huber-loss"></a>

### Huber Loss

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Behave like squared error for small residuals and absolute error for large residuals.

**Explanation:**

Huber loss behaves like squared error for small errors and more like absolute error for large errors, balancing smoothness and robustness to outliers. Quantile loss, also called pinball loss, assigns different costs to overestimation and underestimation to learn a conditional quantile. Inventory planning, for example, may require a conservative high-demand quantile as well as average demand. Choose a loss based on what should be predicted and the costs of different errors, rather than the popularity of an abbreviation.

Interview answer: BCE is used for binary probability predictions and strongly penalizes confidently wrong predictions. Mutually exclusive multiclass tasks commonly use multiclass cross-entropy. For continuous-value prediction, consider MSE, MAE or Huber loss. Model architecture and loss function are separate choices; the same network can be trained with different objectives.

**Boundary and distinctions:** The transition scale still needs to suit the task.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [MSE / MAE / RMSE](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-mse-mae-rmse) — Large-error penalties differ from robustness choices

<a id="concept-initialization-residual-connection"></a>

### Initialization / Residual Connection

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Initialization chooses starting parameter values; residual connections let a branch learn a change relative to its input.

**Explanation:**

Initialization determines the starting point of training. Using the same weights for all neurons may not break the symmetry; the scale may be too large or too small, making it difficult to propagate information and gradients. Xavier and He initialization are common methods for selecting initial scales based on layer structure and activation properties. They help get started with training and do not directly impart knowledge to the model. The weights of the pre-trained model have come from learning, which is not the same thing as random initialization.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Residual connections are covered in Chapter 49; neither mechanism represents knowledge already learned by the model.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-iteration-optimizer-step-epoch"></a>

### Iteration / Optimizer Step / Epoch

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** An iteration is one loop cycle, an optimizer step is a parameter update, and an epoch usually traverses a finite dataset once.

**Explanation:**

A batch is a collection of samples processed together, and batch size is its sample count. An iteration usually means one execution of the training loop, although the code’s definition matters. An optimizer step is an actual parameter update. An epoch usually means one complete pass through a finite training dataset.

With 1,000 training samples and batches of 100, dropping no samples and updating once per batch gives ten batches and ten parameter updates per epoch. This is one epoch with ten update steps, not ten epochs. With streaming corpora or very large datasets, researchers may report optimizer steps or tokens processed rather than complete passes through the data.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Gradient accumulation or skipped updates means these counts are not interchangeable.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Supports these next concepts:** [Scheduler](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-scheduler)

<a id="concept-kl-divergence"></a>

### KL Divergence

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Measure a directional discrepancy between probability distributions.

**Explanation:**

KL divergence measures a discrepancy between probability distributions. It can train a student model to match a teacher’s distribution or constrain a new policy from moving too far from a reference policy. KL divergence is generally asymmetric, so the direction of comparison matters. It is not a geometric distance or a direct measure of semantic similarity between answers. Cross-entropy, KL divergence and entropy are related, but explain which distributions are being compared rather than treating them as interchangeable losses.

**Boundary and distinctions:** KL divergence is not a symmetric distance, and input conventions depend on the implementation.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.
