<a id="concept-learning-rate"></a>

### Learning Rate

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Control the overall scale of parameter updates, whose actual size also depends on gradients and optimizer state.

**Explanation:**

The learning rate controls the overall step size of optimizer updates. It measures neither how much knowledge has been learned nor how many epochs training has run. Imagine searching for low ground: the update direction tells you where to move, and the learning rate influences how far to move. Optimizers can also use historical gradients to scale individual parameter updates, so the learning rate is not the absolute change applied to every parameter.

If the stride length is too large, it may cross the favorable area at once, oscillate back and forth, and even cause numerical instability in training. Steps that are too small may result in slow improvement within a given budget. There is no single value that is best for all models, batch sizes, and optimizers. A smaller learning rate does not guarantee that the final generalization will be better, because the training budget, data, and other settings jointly affect the results.

Suppose two runs each train for ten epochs. With a learning rate that is too small, one may learn little in that time, while a suitable learning rate gives the other good validation performance. Equal epoch counts do not imply equal optimization progress. Conversely, unstable loss is not always caused by the learning rate: labels, the loss implementation or numerical precision may also be responsible.

**Boundary and distinctions:** The learning rate is neither the epoch count nor a fixed change to every weight.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Gradient](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-gradient)

**Supports these next concepts:** [Scheduler](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-scheduler)

<a id="concept-loss-objective-metric"></a>

### Loss / Objective / Metric

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** A loss supplies a training score, an objective may include additional constraints, and a metric measures task performance.

**Explanation:**

A loss scores model errors and is what training aims to improve. An objective function may also include requirements such as regularization. An evaluation metric indicates whether performance meets the task’s needs. The training objective and reported metric can differ: for example, train a purchase-probability predictor with BCE but assess precision or actual conversion outcomes after deployment. An optimizable loss gives training a direction, without guaranteeing complete alignment with the final business objective.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Reducing the training objective does not guarantee better business metrics.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-microbatch-gradient-accumulation"></a>

### Microbatch / Gradient Accumulation

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Run forward and backward passes on several small batches, then update once after accumulating gradients to reduce peak activation storage.

**Explanation:**

When GPU memory cannot fit many samples at once, split them into microbatches, run forward and backward passes separately, accumulate their gradients and then update. For example, compute gradients after each microbatch but update parameters only after four microbatches: four iterations correspond to one optimizer step. This gives a larger effective batch, but is not always exactly equivalent to one large batch. BatchNorm statistics, for example, can differ. Gradient accumulation does not mean parameters change after every microbatch.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Partial final batches, loss normalization, and BatchNorm can affect equivalence to a large batch.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Batch Size](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-batch-size)

**Related connections:**

- [Zero Grad / Detach](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-zero-grad-detach) — Clearing resets gradient buffers; detaching blocks propagation through a tensor

<a id="concept-mixed-precision-loss-scaling"></a>

### Mixed Precision / Loss Scaling

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Use different numerical precisions for operations; loss scaling helps some low-precision gradients remain representable.

**Explanation:**

These names denote floating-point formats. Lower precision generally saves memory and can accelerate computation on supported hardware, but the numerical range and resolution differ. BF16 has an exponent range similar to FP32 but lower precision; FP16 has a narrower representable range. Mixed precision uses different formats for different operations, often retaining higher precision for sensitive calculations. It does not simply make all numbers smaller, and does not guarantee equal speedups on every device.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Unscaling and optimizer updates must occur at the correct accumulation boundaries.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Dtype / Device](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-dtype-device)

- [Gradient Clipping](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-gradient-clipping) — Unscale gradients before clipping

<a id="concept-mse-mae-rmse"></a>

### MSE / MAE / RMSE

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** MSE emphasizes large errors; MAE is more robust to extreme residuals; RMSE has the same units as the target.

**Explanation:**

MSE, mean squared error, is common in continuous-value prediction and penalizes large errors strongly. MAE, mean absolute error, measures the magnitude of deviations from the true value and is less sensitive to extreme errors. RMSE is the square root of MSE and has the same units as the target. For temperature predictions, an error in degrees is easier to interpret than one in squared degrees. These losses and metrics can be used with other suitable models, not only linear regression.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Account for the target’s units and the different penalties on large errors when choosing or comparing these measures.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Huber Loss](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-huber-loss) — Large-error penalties differ from robustness choices

<a id="concept-nan-inf-oom"></a>

### NaN / Inf / OOM

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** NaN and Inf indicate numerical anomalies; OOM indicates insufficient memory.

**Explanation:**

Loss scaling amplifies the loss in some mixed-precision training so that small gradients remain representable, then compensates before updating. NaN denotes an invalid numeric value; Inf denotes infinity, for example after overflow. These can arise from division by zero, extreme scores or unstable operations. OOM means out of memory, not exploding gradients. For OOM, inspect batch size, sequence length, saved activations and model size. For NaN, inspect numerical values and data first.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Separate numerical diagnosis from memory diagnosis first.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-scheduler"></a>

### Scheduler

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Rules for changing the learning rate based on training progress or validation performance.

**Explanation:**

A learning-rate scheduler specifies how the learning rate changes. Step decay reduces it at specified points; exponential decay reduces it proportionally; cosine annealing follows a smooth cosine curve. ReduceLROnPlateau monitors a metric and lowers the rate when improvement stalls. These rules respond to either a fixed schedule or observed performance. Choose with the total training duration and the need for finer updates near the end in mind.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Specify whether the schedule advances with optimizer updates, iterations, epochs, or validation checks.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Learning Rate](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-learning-rate) · [Iteration / Optimizer Step / Epoch](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-iteration-optimizer-step-epoch)

<a id="concept-sgd-momentum"></a>

### SGD / Momentum

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** SGD uses sampled gradients; momentum incorporates a history of update directions.

**Explanation:**

Full-batch gradient descent uses all training samples to compute an update direction. This gives a less noisy direction but is expensive for large datasets. Strictly, stochastic gradient descent can mean using one sample per update, although modern training commonly uses SGD to mean minibatch training. Minibatches give noisier directions but allow more frequent updates and hardware parallelism. Stochastic gradients are estimates from sampled data, not arbitrary changes to parameters.

**Boundary and distinctions:** In modern use, SGD often means the minibatch version.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Gradient](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-gradient)

- [Adam / AdamW](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-adam-adamw) — Historical directions differ from per-parameter scaling

<a id="concept-train-eval-no-grad"></a>

### Train / Eval / No Grad

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Train and eval modes change the behavior of certain layers; no_grad controls gradient recording.

**Explanation:**

Training and evaluation modes control the behavior of layers such as Dropout and BatchNorm. Disabling gradient recording controls whether the information needed for backpropagation is recorded. These are separate: switching to evaluation mode does not disable every gradient, and disabling gradients does not change Dropout’s training behavior. Set both correctly during evaluation or deployment for stable behavior and efficient resource use.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Evaluation mode and disabling gradients do not replace one another.

<a id="concept-warmup-warm-start"></a>

### Warmup / Warm Start

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Warmup gradually raises the learning rate at the start; a warm start begins from an existing model or state.

**Explanation:**

Warmup first uses a smaller learning rate at the beginning of training, and then gradually increases it to the target level. Its purpose is to get training off to a smoother start, rather than letting the GPU heat up first. Then other scheduling methods are usually added. Not all models must use warmup; warmup that is too long can also eat up the effective training budget. Warmup is different from warm start: the latter usually refers to continuing from an existing model or state, rather than starting over from random initialization.

**Boundary and distinctions:** They describe different mechanisms and can be used together.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-weight-decay"></a>

### Weight Decay

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** Shrink weights during parameter updates to regularize the model.

**Explanation:**

Weight decay discourages excessively large weights. AdamW decouples it from Adam’s adaptive gradient scaling instead of treating it as an ordinary gradient term. For basic SGD, L2 regularization and weight decay can be equivalent under common conditions; that equivalence does not carry over directly to adaptive optimizers. In an interview, explain that the W in AdamW refers to decoupled weight decay, rather than describing it simply as faster Adam.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Weight decay differs from learning-rate decay; equivalence to an L2 penalty depends on the optimizer.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Adam / AdamW](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-adam-adamw) — AdamW decouples weight shrinkage from adaptive gradients

<a id="concept-zero-grad-detach"></a>

### Zero Grad / Detach

**Area:** [Losses, Training, and Optimization](#area-training)

**Definition:** zero_grad clears accumulated gradients; detach cuts a path through which gradients would propagate.

**Explanation:**

Some frameworks accumulate new gradients onto existing ones by default, so clear gradients at the appropriate update boundaries. Failing to clear them can count old gradients again; clearing them too early defeats intended accumulation. Detach and stop-gradient operations block gradient propagation along a path, for example in target networks, teacher branches or unnecessary computation graphs. Detaching does not necessarily copy the underlying data and does not freeze the entire model.

**Boundary and distinctions:** detach does not automatically copy storage or freeze the entire model.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Microbatch / Gradient Accumulation](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-microbatch-gradient-accumulation) — Clearing resets gradient buffers; detaching blocks propagation through a tensor

<a id="concept-attention-transformer"></a>

### Attention / Transformer

**Area:** [LLM Training and Inference](#area-llm)

**Definition:** Attention aggregates information according to relevance; a Transformer organizes sequence computation using attention and related modules.

**Explanation:**

Intuitively, a query represents what the current position seeks, keys provide matching clues at other positions, and values contain the information to aggregate. Attention scores determine aggregation weights after normalization. This is an analogy: queries, keys and values are learned vectors, not human-written questions, catalogs and answers. A high attention weight does not automatically establish interpretable causal importance to the final output.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Attention weights do not automatically provide a causal explanation.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Neural Network](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-neural-network) · [Token / Embedding](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-token-embedding)

**Supports these next concepts:** [SFT / LoRA / QLoRA](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-sft-lora-qlora) · [KV Cache / FlashAttention](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-kv-cache-flashattention)

<a id="concept-dpo-grpo"></a>

### DPO / GRPO

**Area:** [LLM Training and Inference](#area-llm)

**Definition:** DPO typically uses preference pairs; GRPO constructs update signals from relative rewards within sampled groups of outputs.

**Explanation:**

DPO directly optimizes relative response preferences from preference data. Its classic form uses a reference model, without first fitting a separate reward network and then running online policy optimization. IPO, KTO and ORPO are other preference optimization approaches, differing in objectives, feedback formats or dependence on reference models. You need not memorize every objective here. These are methods for training existing models from preferences, rather than new Transformer architectures. Choose according to the available data.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Their feedback formats and sampling/training procedures differ.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [SFT / LoRA / QLoRA](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-sft-lora-qlora) — Supervised and preference training use different feedback

<a id="concept-kv-cache-flashattention"></a>

### KV Cache / FlashAttention

**Area:** [LLM Training and Inference](#area-llm)

**Definition:** A KV cache reuses prefix keys and values; FlashAttention optimizes attention data movement and intermediate storage.

**Explanation:**

The KV cache stores keys and values already computed for processed tokens, avoiding repeated projections of the whole history. Each newly processed token still attends to relevant cached keys and values, so longer context still costs work. Prefix caching reuses computations across requests with a compatible shared prefix and model configuration. User-data isolation still matters: similar-looking text alone does not justify mixing caches.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Cache management, numerical quantization, and kernel optimization are different techniques.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Attention / Transformer](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-attention-transformer)

**Related connections:**

- [Cache](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-cache) — Model-prefix reuse is a specialized cache

<a id="concept-sft-lora-qlora"></a>

### SFT / LoRA / QLoRA

**Area:** [LLM Training and Inference](#area-llm)

**Definition:** SFT defines a supervised training stage and objective; LoRA and QLoRA are adaptation methods with parameter and memory implications.

**Explanation:**

Pretraining learns general patterns from large-scale data. Continued pretraining applies similar objectives to an existing model, often with additional domain data. SFT uses input–expected-response pairs to shape task behavior. These stages can all update parameters but differ in data format and objective. Adding documents does not always require fine-tuning: retrieval can also supply frequently updated knowledge with citations.

**Boundary and distinctions:** A training stage and a parameter-efficient adaptation method describe different aspects.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Attention / Transformer](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-attention-transformer)

<a id="concept-agent"></a>

### Agent

**Area:** [Retrieval, RAG, and Agents](#area-retrieval-agents)

**Definition:** A system that organizes models, tools, feedback, and an execution loop around a goal and state.

**Explanation:**

A fixed workflow arranges major steps such as retrieval, generation and review in advance. An agent loop chooses the next tool or action from current results. ReAct alternates reasoning, action and observation. More autonomous decisions do not necessarily improve reliability. Repeated tasks often suit fixed processes, while open-ended tasks require more dynamic choices. Both can be combined without turning the whole system into an unconstrained loop.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Generating a tool call does not by itself create a reliable task-execution loop.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Network](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-network) — Tool execution must handle external services and failures

<a id="concept-bm25-hnsw"></a>

### BM25 / HNSW

**Area:** [Retrieval, RAG, and Agents](#area-retrieval-agents)

**Definition:** BM25 scores documents using term-matching statistics; HNSW accelerates approximate nearest-neighbor search using a hierarchical graph.

**Explanation:**

An inverted index maps a term to documents containing it, avoiding a full document scan. TF-IDF considers both a term’s prominence within a document and its rarity across the collection. BM25 adds term-frequency saturation and document-length adjustments. Rare product identifiers and exact terminology often suit keyword retrieval; paraphrases with different wording may need semantic representations. BM25 is not a generative language model.

**Boundary and distinctions:** An index cannot compensate for an unsuitable vector representation.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Index](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-index) — Both traditional systems and retrieval locate candidates

<a id="concept-vae-gan-diffusion"></a>

### VAE / GAN / Diffusion

**Area:** [Generative Models and Multimodality](#area-multimodal)

**Definition:** Learn data distribution through different training objectives and generation processes.

**Explanation:**

A VAE maps observations through an encoder to a probability distribution over latent variables, then reconstructs or generates samples with a decoder. Training combines reconstruction with constraints on the latent distribution, making sampling from a simple prior useful. The distinguishing feature is probabilistic latent-variable modeling, not merely dimensionality reduction. Latent variables can be ignored in some settings, so check what information the model actually uses.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Just because they can all generate images does not mean that the training mechanisms are the same.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [World Model](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-world-model) — Realistic generation differs from action-conditioned control

<a id="concept-off-policy-offline-rl"></a>

### Off-policy / Offline RL

**Area:** [Reinforcement and Imitation Learning](#area-rl)

**Definition:** Off-policy methods can learn a target policy from data generated by another policy; offline RL learns from a fixed dataset.

**Explanation:**

Offline RL trains on a fixed collection of interactions without gathering new experience from the environment during training. It can overestimate actions poorly covered by the dataset. CQL addresses this with conservative value estimation; IQL fits values and extracts a policy while limiting dependence on evaluating actions outside the data. Neither creates missing coverage. Offline evaluation is also an imperfect substitute for safe, controlled real-world validation.

**Boundary and distinctions:** An off-policy algorithm can also collect new experience continuously online.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Q-learning / SARSA](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-q-learning-sarsa) — Distinguish policy relationships from data-collection settings

<a id="concept-ppo-sac-td3"></a>

### PPO / SAC / TD3

**Area:** [Reinforcement and Imitation Learning](#area-rl)

**Definition:** PPO typically clips a policy surrogate objective, SAC incorporates entropy regularization, and TD3 reduces overestimation in continuous-action actor–critic learning.

**Explanation:**

TRPO uses a trust-region approach to constrain policy changes and avoid destroying existing behavior in one update. PPO pursues similar stability through easier-to-implement objectives, such as clipping or penalties. It commonly performs several updates on a newly collected batch of interactions before gathering fresh data. PPO controls update incentives; it does not enforce the same maximum change on every parameter or guarantee that a policy never moves too far.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Clipping the PPO objective differs from clipping gradients and does not impose a hard bound on every policy change.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Policy Gradient](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-policy-gradient) — Compare policy- and value-learning objectives and mechanisms

<a id="concept-q-learning-sarsa"></a>

### Q-learning / SARSA

**Area:** [Reinforcement and Imitation Learning](#area-rl)

**Definition:** Q-learning forms updates using a greedy target action; SARSA uses the next action actually taken.

**Explanation:**

Classic Q-learning uses the estimated value of the best next-state action in its target, even when exploration actually selects another action. SARSA uses the value of the action actually selected next under the behavior policy. This illustrates off-policy versus on-policy learning: the relationship between the target policy and the policy collecting data. Off-policy does not mean offline; an off-policy algorithm can collect new data while learning.

**Boundary and distinctions:** They relate the behavior policy and target policy differently.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Bellman Equations](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-bellman)

**Related connections:**

- [Off-policy / Offline RL](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-off-policy-offline-rl) — Distinguish policy relationships from data-collection settings

<a id="concept-dreamer-muzero"></a>

### Dreamer / MuZero

**Area:** [Robotics, VLA, and World Models](#area-embodied)

**Definition:** Dreamer trains policies on imagined trajectories in a learned latent dynamics model; MuZero combines a learned model with search.

**Explanation:**

Dreamer learns a latent world model from real interaction experience, then rolls out imagined trajectories inside that model to train an actor and a critic. It aims to turn each real experience into many internal learning opportunities, improving sample efficiency. The key distinction is training an action policy inside the model; this need not involve a large new search before every real action. Model prediction errors affect the policy, so real data must continually correct the model.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Compare control objectives, prediction targets, and planning mechanisms.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [World Model](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-world-model) — Learned dynamics can support imagination or search

<a id="concept-pid-mpc"></a>

### PID / MPC

**Area:** [Robotics, VLA, and World Models](#area-embodied)

**Definition:** PID uses feedback from error and its history or changes; MPC repeatedly plans under a model and constraints.

**Explanation:**

PID adjusts control using current error, accumulated error and the rate of error change to track a desired state. The proportional term responds to deviation, the integral term handles persistent offset, and the derivative term can provide damping. Noise, delay and tuning affect stability. PID is not learned from large video datasets, but is useful in many stabilization tasks.

**Boundary and distinctions:** The prediction horizon may differ from the executed horizon.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Motion Planning](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-motion-planning) — Planning and feedback control work together

<a id="concept-0-1-knapsack-unbounded-knapsack"></a>

### 0/1 Knapsack / Unbounded Knapsack

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** In 0/1 knapsack each item may be used at most once; unbounded knapsack permits reuse. One-dimensional implementations need the corresponding traversal order.

**Explanation:**

Coin Change and Perfect Squares can use the amount or target value as the state and choose the final denomination or square. Target zero needs zero items; initialize other states as unreachable, then minimize the count using smaller states. Initializing every amount to zero makes unreachable states appear better than valid solutions.

A denomination can be reused, giving an unbounded-knapsack problem. In a one-dimensional implementation that loops over items, capacities are usually processed in increasing order. Minimizing the number of coins is different from counting combinations; for counting, loop order also determines whether different permutations are counted repeatedly.

**Boundary and distinctions:** With items in the outer loop, 0/1 capacities are usually traversed backward and unbounded capacities forward. Also distinguish counting from optimization.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Dynamic Programming](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-dynamic-programming)

<a id="concept-backtracking-pruning"></a>

### Backtracking / Pruning

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Explore a choice tree, undo path state on return, and prune branches that cannot produce valid answers.

**Explanation:**

Backtracking expands choices into a search tree: choose, explore recursively, then undo the choice on return. Permutations use a used marker so each element is chosen once. Subsets use an increasing start index so different selection orders do not enumerate the same set repeatedly. Define the state first, then choose used markers, a starting index, or a remaining target.

Copying the current path is usually required when adding it to an answer. If you only save a reference to the same mutable list, undoing it later will change all answers together. Backtracking is not an antonym of dynamic programming; memoization is also possible when different search paths have the same subsequent state.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Pruning depends on the problem constraints, and enumeration cost is also bounded below by the output size.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Recursion](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-recursion)

<a id="concept-canonical-key"></a>

### Canonical Key

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Eliminate unimportant representation differences and generate identical index keys for the same equivalence class.

**Explanation:**

The difficulty with anagram grouping is not how to append the list, but constructing the same keys for the same class of objects. The sorted character sequence can be used as the key; when the question is limited to lowercase English letters, the twenty-six character count can also be used as the key. For example, the character order of eat and tea is different, but the frequency array is the same. This idea is called normalized representation: eliminating unimportant order differences.

Keys must be unambiguous. Do not concatenate multiple counts into a number string without separation, otherwise different counts may result in the same string. Sorting keys incur additional character sorting costs; counting keys for a fixed alphabet can be constructed linearly based on the total number of characters, but the twenty-six position premise cannot be directly generalized to all character sets.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Character counts can identify anagrams. Composite keys must encode those counts unambiguously.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-dummy-node"></a>

### Dummy Node

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Place an auxiliary node before a linked list’s actual head so changes at the head and elsewhere can use the same pointer operations.

**Explanation:**

Linked list questions need to distinguish between node identity and node value. Two nodes with the same value do not mean that the linked lists intersect. The sentinel or dummy node is placed before the real head, so that operations such as deleting the head node and inserting the head can also be written as "modify the next of the predecessor". When deleting the nth node from the last, the fast and slow pointers maintain a fixed distance, so that the slow pointer finally falls on the predecessor of the node to be deleted. The bounds should be derived from loop invariants, not just by reciting how many times the fast pointer has been moved.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Return the actual head node; do not use sentinel values as input data.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-fast-and-slow-pointers"></a>

### Fast and Slow Pointers

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Use different pointer speeds to find a midpoint or detect a cycle, then equal speeds to locate its entry.

**Explanation:**

A fast pointer taking two steps and a slow pointer taking one can find a midpoint or detect a cycle. Without a cycle, the fast pointer reaches null first; with a cycle, the pointers must meet inside it. To find the cycle entry, reset one pointer to the head, then advance both at the same speed. Their next meeting point is the entry. This follows from the relationship between the head-to-entry distance and distances around the cycle.

To test whether a linked list is a palindrome, find a midpoint, reverse the second half, and compare corresponding values using constant auxiliary space. Restore the second half if the caller expects the input unchanged. The pointer initialization determines which of the two middle nodes is selected for an even-length list.

**Boundary and distinctions:** The first meeting point is usually not the cycle entry, and null checks remain necessary.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-in-place-marking"></a>

### In-place Marking

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Use part of the input storage to record pending operations or visited state, reducing auxiliary space.

**Explanation:**

When setting zero in a matrix, you cannot immediately change the rows and columns as soon as you see zero, otherwise the newly created zeros will continue to propagate. First record which rows and columns need to be changed to zero, and then execute them uniformly. To compress the mark space, you can use the first row and first column as marks, but you should save whether the first row and first column originally contain zeros. Process the first row and column last to avoid overwriting the mark before it is used up.

**Boundary and distinctions:** This modifies the input. Preserve information in marker positions or process it in a safe order.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-kadane"></a>

### Kadane’s Algorithm

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Maintain the largest nonempty subarray sum ending at the current position, choosing whether to extend the previous subarray or start a new one.

**Explanation:**

Maximum subarray sum can define the state as "the largest non-empty consecutive sum that must end at the current position". The new element is either connected to the previous interval or starts over; choose the larger value between the two, and then use the global answer to record the maximum value among all end points. The state only needs the previous value, so it can be squeezed into constant extra space.

For [-2,3,-1,4], the best sum ending at the final position comes from [3,-1,4]. If every value is negative, choose the largest negative value. Initializing the answer to zero would incorrectly allow an empty subarray.

**Boundary and distinctions:** An all-negative array still needs to return a negative number, which cannot be replaced by an empty interval of zero.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-loop-invariant"></a>

### Loop Invariant

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** State a property that holds before the loop starts and is preserved by each iteration, then use it with the termination condition to establish correctness.

**Explanation:**

Two pointers are more than merely writing two indices. The positions must represent processed boundaries, current candidates, or traversals at different speeds, and each move must preserve all possible answers. A loop invariant describes a property that holds before and after every iteration. In Move Zeroes, the region before the write pointer always contains the nonzero elements retained in their original order; the read pointer keeps looking for the next element.

To preserve nonzero elements in place and in their original order, write them to the front and then fill the remainder with zeros. A swap-based version should not advance the write pointer when it reads zero. Linear time and constant auxiliary space permit more than one pass; two simple scans still meet those bounds.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Examples alone do not prove it; explain why every move preserves possible answers.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-lower-bound-upper-bound"></a>

### Lower Bound / Upper Bound

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** In a sorted sequence, lower bound finds the first value at least the target, and upper bound finds the first value greater than it. Their difference counts occurrences.

**Explanation:**

Binary search relies on a monotonic true/false condition, rather than merely a sorted array. To find an insertion position, search for the first value greater than or equal to the target. With a half-open interval [left,right), initialize right to the array length. If the midpoint satisfies the condition, keep the left part including that midpoint; otherwise move left just past it. The search ends when left equals right, giving the boundary.

The invariant must preserve the desired boundary, which may equal the array length. Keep the termination and update rules consistent with either a half-open or a closed search interval. For fixed-width integers, computing the midpoint as left plus half of right-left can avoid the overflow of left+right.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Interval conventions and updates must agree. A boundary position does not itself prove the target exists.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Supports these next concepts:** [Binary Search on the Answer](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-binary-search-answer) · [Consistent Hashing](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-consistent-hashing)

<a id="concept-monotonic-deque"></a>

### Monotonic Deque

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Maintain candidate indices for window extrema in a deque and remove expired candidates from the front.

**Explanation:**

For a sliding-window maximum, a deque stores indices in nonincreasing order of their values. When a new value arrives, remove indices from the back while their values are no greater: the new value is at least as large and expires later. Remove the front index when it leaves the window. The remaining front gives the current maximum.

For example, the window sweeps through one, three, and two. When three enters, one can be eliminated, but two cannot eliminate three. Each index can enter and exit the queue once at most, so the amortized time is linear. Use a queue that supports constant-time operations on both ends; deleting the head of an ordinary array in some languages will move elements, and it cannot be claimed that the implementation is still linear.

**Boundary and distinctions:** This differs from a monotonic stack. Linear-time array-front deletion can degrade the implementation.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-monotonic-stack"></a>

### Monotonic Stack

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Store unresolved candidates and pop those whose answers become determined when a new element arrives.

**Explanation:**

Daily Temperatures maintains a stack of indices with nonincreasing temperatures. When a warmer temperature arrives, repeatedly pop indices; the difference between the current index and the popped index is the waiting time. The stack contains positions whose answers are unresolved, and popped positions need no further work. Each index is pushed and popped once, giving linear total work by amortized analysis. Equal temperature is not warmer, so it must not resolve an earlier position.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Linear total work follows because each item enters and leaves at most once. Specify comparisons for equal values.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-multi-source-bfs"></a>

### Multi-source BFS

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Initialize several sources at distance zero and expand by BFS layers to find earliest arrival in an equal-weight graph.

**Explanation:**

For Rotting Oranges, enqueue all initially rotten cells at time zero. One BFS level represents one minute; the first time a fresh orange is reached is its rotting time. Track the number of fresh oranges remaining. If any remain after traversal, they are unreachable. With no fresh oranges initially, the answer is zero.

The earliest arrival conclusion of BFS relies on each propagation edge taking the same time. If the propagation time of different grids is different, methods such as weighted shortest path must be considered, and the number of layers cannot be directly regarded as time.

**Boundary and distinctions:** With unequal edge travel times, layer count need not equal shortest travel time.

<a id="concept-postorder-dp"></a>

### Postorder DP

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Compute subtree summaries first, then form the value returned to the parent or a global candidate answer.

**Explanation:**

Maximum depth returns the larger child depth plus one to the parent. Diameter updates a global answer at each node using the sum of its left and right depths, but returns only a one-sided depth. Maximum Path Sum needs the same distinction: a node can join both sides when updating the global answer, but a path passed to its parent can extend along only one side and cannot branch.

When calculating the maximum path sum, negative subtree contributions are not required, but negative numbers should be allowed in the global answer, otherwise a fully negative tree will return zero by mistake. The diameter is usually calculated by the number of edges, and the depth is usually calculated by the number of nodes. The initialization and increment must be consistent with the definition.

**Boundary and distinctions:** A one-sided path passed upward differs from a candidate joining both sides at the current node.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Recursion](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-recursion)

<a id="concept-prefix-sum"></a>

### Prefix Sum

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Store cumulative sums at boundaries and obtain a range sum by subtracting two prefixes.

**Explanation:**

Define the prefix sum P such that the sum of the first zero elements is zero. The sum of a segment is k, which is equivalent to the current prefix sum minus an earlier prefix sum equal to k. Therefore, when scanning the current prefix P, check how many times P minus k has appeared before, then accumulate the answer, and finally record the current P. The occurrence of the zero prefix must be recorded once at the beginning to count the interval starting from the beginning of the array.

For example, one, negative one, one, the target is one. The three legal intervals come from two single elements and the entire array; the prefix frequency can count the contribution of repeated prefixes. The hash table must save the number of times, not just whether it exists. Recording the current prefix first and then querying will incorrectly include empty intervals when k is zero.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Counting often needs prefix frequencies and an initial zero prefix. Tree paths also need state undo on return.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-quickselect-top-k"></a>

### Quickselect / Top K

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Quickselect recurses or iterates only into the partition containing the target rank. A bounded heap can instead maintain the current Top K in a stream.

**Explanation:**

If you want to find the kth largest value, you don't have to sort the entire array. Maintain a min-heap with a size of at most k. The top of the heap is the minimum value among the current retainers, which is the elimination threshold. It is worth replacing only if the new value exceeds the threshold. After scanning, the top of the heap will be the kth largest. The frequencies of the top k high-frequency elements are first counted, and then the same selection is made according to the frequency. The ranking object changes from the numerical value to the frequency of the key.

The heap only guarantees the extreme value at the top of the heap, and does not guarantee the overall ordering of the internal array. Here, the kth largest number of elements is counted, and repeated values still account for multiple rankings; the top k high-frequency objects are different keys and must be distinguished.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Quickselect usually modifies input. Randomized versions have expected linear but worst-case quadratic time.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

<a id="concept-sliding-window"></a>

### Sliding Window

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Maintain a contiguous interval and incremental state such as frequencies, searching through expansion and contraction.

**Explanation:**

The sliding window maintains a contiguous interval, allowing the right end to incorporate new elements, the left end to remove old elements, and incrementally update status such as frequency. First define when the current range is legal, and then decide when to shrink. In the longest substring without repeated characters, once a new character causes repetition, the window will continue to be narrowed until there are no more repetitions, and then the maximum length will be updated.

For example, on the second b in abba, move left past both the leading a and the first b; removing just one character is insufficient. If using last-seen indices, set left to the maximum of its current value and the repeated character’s previous index plus one. This prevents left from moving backward at the final a.

**Boundary and distinctions:** With negative values, interval sums are not monotonic under expansion; positive-array window rules do not apply unchanged.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Loop Invariant](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-loop-invariant)

**Related connections:**

- [Two Pointers](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-two-pointers) — Windows maintain pointers over contiguous intervals
- [Monotonic Deque](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-monotonic-deque) — Candidate deques maintain window extrema

<a id="concept-topological-sort"></a>

### Topological Sort

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Order vertices to satisfy precedence constraints in a directed acyclic graph.

**Explanation:**

For Course Schedule, encode prerequisites as directed edges. Enqueue every zero-in-degree vertex, process it, and decrement its successors’ in-degrees. Enqueue a successor when its in-degree reaches zero. All courses are feasible exactly when all vertices are processed; otherwise the remaining graph contains a directed cycle. Include isolated courses in the total.

A DFS alternative uses visitation colors. Encountering a vertex that is still on the active recursion path reveals a directed cycle; encountering a fully processed vertex does not. A topological order exists only for a DAG. Ordinary BFS without dependency bookkeeping does not provide this test.

**Boundary and distinctions:** If the in-degree algorithm cannot process every vertex, a directed cycle exists. Encountering a previously visited vertex alone is insufficient evidence.

**Recommended prerequisites:** No explicit prerequisite edge in this map.

**Related connections:**

- [Graph Algorithms](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-graph-algorithms) — Indegrees organize directed dependencies

<a id="concept-two-pointers"></a>

### Two Pointers

**Area:** [Hot 100 Algorithm Practice](#area-hot100)

**Definition:** Assign two positions boundary or candidate roles and eliminate repeated enumeration through safe movement.

**Explanation:**

Two pointers are more than merely writing two indices. The positions must represent processed boundaries, current candidates, or traversals at different speeds, and each move must preserve all possible answers. A loop invariant describes a property that holds before and after every iteration. In Move Zeroes, the region before the write pointer always contains the nonzero elements retained in their original order; the read pointer keeps looking for the next element.

To preserve nonzero elements in place and in their original order, write them to the front and then fill the remainder with zeros. A swap-based version should not advance the write pointer when it reads zero. Linear time and constant auxiliary space permit more than one pass; two simple scans still meet those bounds.

**Boundary and distinctions:** Two indices are not a proof; justify moves using ordering, bounds, or another elimination argument.

**Recommended prerequisites:** [Loop Invariant](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-loop-invariant)

**Related connections:**

- [Sliding Window](KNOWLEDGE_MAP.md#concept-sliding-window) — Windows maintain pointers over contiguous intervals
